concepts.title: Thermal Equilibrium and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.definition: When two distinct thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system separately, they are also in mutual thermal equilibrium with one another.
concepts.formula: T_A = T_C and T_B = T_C implies T_A = T_B
concepts.key_idea: Equality of temperature is the defining requirement for thermal equilibrium between contacting systems.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: state the zeroth law of thermodynamics and its significance
explain how the zeroth law of thermodynamics leads to the definition of temperature
if system A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, what can be inferred about A and B
describe thermal equilibrium between two thermodynamic systems separated by a diathermic wall
verify whether two bodies at different initial temperatures attain thermal equilibrium when brought into contact

solution_steps.explain: Determine whether systems are separated by insulating adiabatic walls or conducting diathermic walls.
Conclude that independent thermal equilibria with a common system ensure equal temperature values across all systems.

solution_steps.action: verify temperature equality across the systems
solution_steps.explain: Confirm that the inferred common temperature value is consistent for all systems in contact, establishing thermal equilibrium.

concepts.title: First Law of Thermodynamics and Energy Conservation
concepts.definition: Energy supplied to a system as heat is distributed between raising its internal energy and performing mechanical work on the environment.
concepts.key_idea: Internal energy change depends solely on net heat transferred minus work done by the system.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate the change in internal energy when heat input and work output are given
find the change in internal energy of a system absorbing heat and doing work
determine the heat added to a system given internal energy increase and work done
compute the work done by a system when heat supplied and internal energy change are known
evaluate internal energy change delta_U from heat added delta_Q and work done delta_W

solution_steps.action: subtract work done from heat supplied
solution_steps.explain: Apply energy conservation delta_U = delta_Q - delta_W to find internal energy change.

solution_steps.action: verify the sign convention for work and heat
solution_steps.explain: heat added to the system is positive and work done by the system is positive so a net energy increase gives a positive delta_U

solution_steps.action: express the internal energy change with units
solution_steps.explain: state the computed change in internal energy in joules for the given heat input and work output

worked_examples.answer: First Law of Thermodynamics and Energy Conservation applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.question: Apply first law of thermodynamics and energy conservation to a fresh example and interpret the result.

worked_examples.answer: The method of first law of thermodynamics and energy conservation leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Work Done in Isobaric Expansion
concepts.definition: Mechanical work performed by an expanding gas maintained under constant external pressure equals the product of pressure and total volume change.
concepts.key_idea: Under constant pressure conditions, work done is directly proportional to the change in volume.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: compute work done by a gas during isobaric expansion
calculate work done when a gas expands from an initial volume to a final volume at constant pressure
find the work done by a system changing volume under constant pressure
determine mechanical work performed during volume expansion at constant pressure
what is the work done against a constant pressure when volume increases

solution_steps.explain: Subtract initial volume from final volume to get volume shift delta_V.
Calculate work by multiplying constant pressure by volume change.

solution_steps.action: express the work done with units
solution_steps.explain: state the computed isobaric work in joules for the given pressure and volume change

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving work done in isobaric expansion.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: calculate change in volume. Step 2: multiply pressure by volume change. Step 3: express the work done with units. Working: final_volume - initial_volume, pressure * delta_v, work.
worked_examples.answer: Work Done in Isobaric Expansion applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.question: Apply work done in isobaric expansion to a fresh example and interpret the result.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: calculate change in volume. Step 2: multiply pressure by volume change. Step 3: express the work done with units. Working: final_volume - initial_volume, pressure * delta_v, work.
worked_examples.answer: The method of work done in isobaric expansion leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Heat Transfer and Specific Heat Capacity
concepts.definition: Thermal energy required to modify the temperature of a substance is the product of its mass, specific heat capacity, and temperature variation.
concepts.key_idea: Specific heat capacity quantifies energy needed per unit mass for one degree temperature change.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: find the heat required to change temperature of a given mass
calculate thermal energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance
determine heat energy absorbed when mass, specific heat, and temperature rise are provided
compute total heat transferred to a body given mass and temperature difference
what is the heat required to elevate temperature of a sample of known mass

solution_steps.action: multiply mass, specific heat, and temperature change
solution_steps.explain: Apply heat capacity relation heat = mass * sp_heat * delta_T.

solution_steps.action: determine the direction of heat flow
solution_steps.explain: a positive heat value indicates heat absorbed during heating while a negative value indicates heat released during cooling

solution_steps.action: express the heat transferred with units
solution_steps.explain: state the computed heat energy in joules for the given mass and temperature change

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving heat transfer and specific heat capacity.

worked_examples.answer: Heat Transfer and Specific Heat Capacity applied step by step gives the required result.

concepts.title: Mayer's Relation for Ideal Gas Specific Heats
concepts.definition: For an ideal gas, molar specific heat capacity at constant pressure exceeds molar specific heat capacity at constant volume by the universal gas constant.
concepts.key_idea: Constant pressure heating requires additional energy to compensate for expansion work against external pressure.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate molar specific heat at constant pressure using Mayer's relation
find Cp given Cv and universal gas constant R
determine molar heat capacity at constant volume Cv from Cp and R
compute molar heat capacity at constant pressure for an ideal gas
apply Mayer's formula to find constant pressure heat capacity

solution_steps.action: add universal gas constant to constant volume heat capacity
solution_steps.explain: Use Mayer's relation Cp = Cv + R to obtain constant pressure molar heat capacity.
constant pressure heating requires extra energy for expansion work so Cp must be greater than Cv by the gas constant R

solution_steps.action: express the molar heat capacity with units
solution_steps.explain: state the computed constant pressure molar heat capacity in joules per mole per kelvin

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving mayer's relation for ideal gas specific heats.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: add universal gas constant to constant volume heat capacity. Step 2: verify that Cp exceeds Cv. Step 3: express the molar heat capacity with units. Working: cv + r, cp.
worked_examples.answer: Mayer's Relation for Ideal Gas Specific Heats applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.question: Apply mayer's relation for ideal gas specific heats to a fresh example and interpret the result.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: add universal gas constant to constant volume heat capacity. Step 2: verify that Cp exceeds Cv. Step 3: express the molar heat capacity with units. Working: cv + r, cp.
worked_examples.answer: The method of mayer's relation for ideal gas specific heats leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Thermodynamic State Variables and Classification
concepts.definition: Variables describing equilibrium states are categorized as extensive when proportional to system dimensions, or intensive when independent of system size.
concepts.key_idea: Dividing a system in equilibrium leaves intensive variables unaltered while extensive variables scale proportionally.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: differentiate between extensive and intensive thermodynamic variables
classify pressure, volume, temperature, and internal energy as extensive or intensive
explain why heat and work are path dependent and not state variables
what defines a thermodynamic state variable and an equation of state
verify whether internal energy is an extensive state variable

solution_steps.explain: Imagine splitting the system into equal halves; variables that remain unchanged are intensive, while halved variables are extensive.

solution_steps.action: classify each variable as extensive or intensive
solution_steps.explain: pressure and temperature remain unchanged on partitioning so they are intensive, while volume, mass, and internal energy are halved so they are extensive.

solution_steps.action: verify that heat and work are not state variables
solution_steps.explain: heat and work depend on the path taken between states rather than the state itself, so they are not thermodynamic state variables.

concepts.title: Work Done in Adiabatic Expansion of Ideal Gas
concepts.definition: During energy transfer without heat exchange, work executed by an ideal gas equals the decrease in internal energy calculated from initial and final temperatures.
concepts.key_idea: Adiabatic work output draws directly on internal thermal energy, producing a drop in temperature.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate work done by ideal gas in adiabatic process
find work done during adiabatic change from initial temperature T1 to final temperature T2
determine mechanical work in adiabatic expansion given moles, adiabatic index, and temperatures
compute adiabatic work done using initial and final temperatures
what is the work done by an ideal gas undergoing adiabatic expansion

solution_steps.explain: Subtract final temperature T2 from initial temperature T1.
Subtract 1 from ratio of specific heats gamma.
Multiply moles, gas constant, and delta_T, then divide by gamma factor.

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving work done in adiabatic expansion of ideal gas.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: compute temperature difference. Step 2: compute adiabatic factor. Step 3: calculate adiabatic work done. Working: t1 - t2, gamma - 1, moles * r * delta_t / gamma_factor.
worked_examples.answer: Work Done in Adiabatic Expansion of Ideal Gas applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.question: Apply work done in adiabatic expansion of ideal gas to a fresh example and interpret the result.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: compute temperature difference. Step 2: compute adiabatic factor. Step 3: calculate adiabatic work done. Working: t1 - t2, gamma - 1, moles * r * delta_t / gamma_factor.
worked_examples.answer: The method of work done in adiabatic expansion of ideal gas leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Work Done in Cyclic Thermodynamic Process
concepts.definition: In a closed thermodynamic cycle, overall internal energy variation is zero, making net work performed equal to the area enclosed on a pressure-volume diagram.
concepts.key_idea: Total work in a cyclic process corresponds to the area within the closed PV loop.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate total work done in a cyclic process
find net work done in a triangular cycle on a pressure volume diagram
determine work output from a cyclic PV diagram
compute enclosed area to find net work done in a thermodynamic cycle
what is the net work done by a gas completing a cyclic path

solution_steps.explain: Subtract minimum volume V1 from maximum volume V2.
Subtract minimum pressure P1 from maximum pressure P2.
Multiply half the volume span by pressure span to calculate enclosed cyclic work.

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving work done in cyclic thermodynamic process.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: calculate volume span. Step 2: calculate pressure span. Step 3: calculate enclosed triangular work area. Working: v2 - v1, p2 - p1, 0.5 * delta_v * delta_p.
worked_examples.answer: Work Done in Cyclic Thermodynamic Process applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.question: Apply work done in cyclic thermodynamic process to a fresh example and interpret the result.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: calculate volume span. Step 2: calculate pressure span. Step 3: calculate enclosed triangular work area. Working: v2 - v1, p2 - p1, 0.5 * delta_v * delta_p.
worked_examples.answer: The method of work done in cyclic thermodynamic process leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics Statements
concepts.definition: The second law asserts that thermal energy cannot spontaneously transfer from cold to hot bodies (Clausius) and complete conversion of heat to work in a cycle is impossible (Kelvin-Planck).
concepts.key_idea: No real or ideal cyclic heat engine can convert absorbed heat entirely into mechanical work.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: state Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics
state Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics
explain why 100 percent efficiency is impossible for heat engines
show the equivalence between Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements
verify why heat cannot spontaneously transfer from cold to hot reservoir

solution_steps.explain: Verify that complete heat-to-work conversion or unassisted heat flow from cold to hot both violate fundamental thermodynamic directionality.
confirm that the engine efficiency is strictly less than one, meaning some heat must always be rejected to the sink.

solution_steps.action: confirm equivalence of the two statements
solution_steps.explain: show that violating the Kelvin-Planck statement leads to a violation of the Clausius statement and vice versa, establishing their equivalence.

concepts.title: Reversible and Irreversible Processes
concepts.definition: A process is reversible if both system and surroundings return to initial states along the exact reverse path; presence of dissipative factors or non-equilibrium states induces irreversibility.
concepts.key_idea: Reversibility demands quasi-static progress and complete absence of friction or viscosity.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes
what conditions make a thermodynamic process reversible
explain why free expansion of a gas is an irreversible process
list main factors that cause irreversibility in natural processes
verify whether quasi-static expansion with friction is reversible

solution_steps.explain: Confirm whether the process occurs infinitely slowly without dissipative losses like friction or turbulence.
look for friction, viscosity, turbulence, or finite temperature gradients that prevent the system from passing through equilibrium states.

solution_steps.action: classify the process as reversible or irreversible
solution_steps.explain: if both quasi-static and non-dissipative conditions hold the process is reversible, otherwise it is irreversible.

concepts.title: Efficiency of Carnot Heat Engine
concepts.definition: The maximum theoretical efficiency of a reversible heat engine operating between two reservoirs depends exclusively on source and sink absolute temperatures.
concepts.key_idea: Carnot efficiency sets the upper limit for heat-to-work conversion between two temperature limits.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate efficiency of a Carnot engine
find Carnot efficiency operating between source temperature T1 and sink temperature T2
determine the efficiency of a reversible heat engine operating between two temperatures
compute thermal efficiency of Carnot cycle given source and sink absolute temperatures
what is the maximum possible efficiency for an engine working between two thermal reservoirs

solution_steps.explain: Divide cold sink absolute temperature T_sink by hot source absolute temperature T_source.
Subtract temperature ratio from 1 to determine thermal efficiency.

solution_steps.action: express the efficiency as a percentage
solution_steps.explain: multiply the efficiency by 100 to express the Carnot engine efficiency in percent

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving efficiency of carnot heat engine.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: compute temperature ratio. Step 2: calculate efficiency. Step 3: express the efficiency as a percentage. Working: t_sink / t_source, 1 - ratio, efficiency * 100.
worked_examples.answer: Efficiency of Carnot Heat Engine applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.answer: The method of efficiency of carnot heat engine leads to the required value or conclusion.

concepts.title: Heat Transfer Ratio in Carnot Engine
concepts.definition: In a Carnot cycle, heat absorbed from the hot source and heat rejected to the cold sink are directly proportional to their respective absolute temperatures.
concepts.key_idea: Absolute thermodynamic temperatures dictate exact heat exchange proportions in ideal reversible cycles.
question_patterns: in Class 11 thermodynamics: calculate heat rejected to sink by Carnot engine
find heat released Q2 given heat absorbed Q1 and reservoir temperatures
determine heat transferred to cold reservoir in a Carnot cycle
compute rejected heat Q_sink from source heat Q_source and temperatures T_source and T_sink
what is the heat exhausted to sink in a reversible engine

solution_steps.explain: Divide sink temperature T_sink by source temperature T_source.
Multiply absorbed heat Q_source by temperature ratio.

solution_steps.action: express the rejected heat with units
solution_steps.explain: state the computed heat rejected to the cold sink in joules for the given absorbed heat and reservoir temperatures

worked_examples.answer: Heat Transfer Ratio in Carnot Engine applied step by step gives the required result.

worked_examples.solution: Step 1: compute absolute temperature ratio. Step 2: calculate heat rejected to sink. Step 3: express the rejected heat with units. Working: t_sink / t_source, q_source * temp_ratio, q_sink.
worked_examples.answer: The method of heat transfer ratio in carnot engine leads to the required value or conclusion.
